[![](data:image/png;base64,)](http://crossmark.crossref.org/dialog/?doi=10.1016/j.ijbiomac.2025.139947&domain=pdf)Polydopamine-modified sodium alginate hydrogel for microplastics removal: Adsorption performance, characteristics, and kinetics

Mengzhen Han , Zihan Wang , Ziyue Xie , Mengxin Hou , Zhenpeng Gao [\*](#_bookmark0)

_College of Food Science and Engineering, Northwest A&F University, 712100 Yangling, Shaanxi, China_

A R T I C L E I N F O

_Keywords:_

Sodium alginate hydrogel Microplastics

Adsorption Polydopamine

A B S T R A C T

The potential health hazards of micro/nanoplastics in food have become a significant concern. This study developed a Polydopamine-modified sodium alginate hydrogel (PMSAH) for removing microplastics in daily drinking water. The hydrogel’s performance, characteristics, and kinetics for microplastic removal were sys-tematically evaluated. Results demonstrated that the incorporation of polydopamine reduced the hydrogel’s surface zeta potential and increased its adsorption capacity for microplastics. PMSAH5 exhibited the highest removal efficiency, reaching approximately 99.6 %. Additionally, polydopamine-modified sodium alginate hydrogel exhibited higher elasticity and thermal stability. The hydrogel successfully adsorbed microplastics, regardless of their size and surface charge. This adsorption was driven by the combined action of multiple forces, resulting in multilayer adsorption. The unique advantages of polydopamine-mediated multi-molecular in-teractions present a promising and environmentally friendly approach for effective removal of microplastics in daily drinking water.

# Introduction

Plastic products play a pervasive role in food packaging and storage applications. The potential release of microplastics into water during routine use of plastic products is documented concern \[[1](#_bookmark11)\]. Studies reveal that the major source of human ingestion of micro—/nanoplastics is drinking water (bottled and tap water), accounting for 88 % of known sources \[[2](#_bookmark12)\]. Microplastics are considered to be plastic particles with dimensions smaller than 5 mm, taking the form of fragments, particles, or fibers \[[1](#_bookmark11)\]. Recent research indicates that plastic degradation extends beyond the micrometer level, breaking down into nanoscale particles \[[1](#_bookmark11)\]. Single microplastic particles can produce millions to billions of nanoscale plastic particles. Nanoplastics typically refer to plastic frag-

ments, particles, or fibers with diameters <100 nm. Nanoplastics may

have a broader and higher distribution in the environment \[[3](#_bookmark13)\]. The potential health hazards of micro/nanoplastics in food have become a significant concern. Extensive animal studies suggest that exposure to micro/nanoplastics induces alterations in gut microbiota, immune cell toxicity, pulmonary toxicity, neurotoxicity, reproductive and genetic toxicity, as well as adverse effects on blood components like red blood cells and vascular endothelial cells \[[4](#_bookmark14)\]. Therefore, the development of an effective method for removing microplastics from water is deemed

essential.

Currently, the removal methods of microplastics from industrial wastewater involves bioremediation, membrane bioreactors (MBR), electrocoagulation, sol-gel technology, flotation, and enhanced filtra-tion \[[5](#_bookmark15)\]. However, these methods are not suitable for everyday house-hold use. Adsorption is one of the most attractive microplastics removal technique for everyday household use due to its simplicity, safety, effi-ciency, and cost-effectiveness \[[6](#_bookmark16)\]. In recent years, various adsorption materials such as sponges, foams, chitosan, oxidized graphene, and biochar have been reported \[[7](#_bookmark17)\]. However, considering the material and energy costs, as well as the significant heterogeneity of microplastics in terms of chemical composition, morphology, density, and surface charge, there is currently no practical technology that can universally and rapidly capture microplastics. Therefore, developing safe and convenient materials that can universally and rapidly capture various types of microplastics in daily drinking water has significant commercial potential.

Hydrogel materials with a three-dimensional network structure offer advantageous porous configurations that facilitate the easy diffusion of small molecules into their internal structure \[[8](#_bookmark18)\]. Simultaneously, the unique swelling properties of hydrogels allow them not only to adsorb pollutants on their surface but also within the three-dimensional

network structure during the process of removing water contaminants \[[8](#_bookmark18)\]. Sodium alginate, as a naturally occurring anionic polysaccharide, has garnered widespread attention due to its abundant source, low cost, good biocompatibility, biodegradability, and excellent heavy metal chelation capabilities \[[9](#_bookmark19)\]. Thus, sodium alginate hydrogel can serve as an effective biodegradable material for removing microplastics. Poly-dopamine (PDA), formed through the self-polymerization of dopamine in a weak alkaline aqueous solution, is a polymer rich in hydrophilic groups such as amino, hydroxyl, and carboxyl groups, along with hy-drophobic groups like the aromatic ring \[[10](#_bookmark20)\]. Consequently, Polydop-amine (PDA) can adhere to the substrate surface based on substrate characteristics through electrostatic forces, hydrogen bonding, hydro-phobic interactions, and π-π stacking or covalent bonding \[[6](#_bookmark16)\]. Hence, it can be inferred that PDA-modified sodium alginate hydrogel enhances the adsorption of microplastics through interfacial interactions.

In this research, we aimed to develop polydopamine (PDA)-modified sodium alginate hydrogels for routine use in food products to remove various microplastics. We investigated the impact of incorporating PDA fibers into the sodium alginate hydrogels and its influence on the adsorption capacity for microplastics. Specifically, our focus was on the particles released from non-woven fabric tea bags after immersion in hot water (95 ◦C) for 15 min under typical usage conditions. To further explore the adsorption characteristics of PMSAH on various micro-plastics, microplastics with different surface charges (negative or posi-tive) and sizes ranging from 200 nm to 10 μm were employed to understand the capturing process. Finally, PMSAH was further used to investigate the adsorption isotherms and kinetics of carboxylated poly-styrene nanospheres and amino-functionalized polystyrene nano-spheres, which represent negative and positive microplastics, respectively.

# Materials and methods

- 1.  _Materials_

Sodium alginate (CAS No. 9005-38-3, mannuronate/guluronate = 1:1, viscosity 200 ± 20 MPa.s, MV: 107335.5) was procured from Aladdin (Shanghai, China). Dopamine hydrochloride (CAS No. 62–31-7, purity: 98 %, MV: 189.64) was provided by Shanghai Macklin Biochemical Technology Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China). Calcium chloride dihydrate (CAS No. 10035–04-8, MV: 147 g/mol) was obtained from China National Chemical Corporation (Beijing, China). Non-woven fabric tea bags, polyethylene microspheres **(PE 10)** (10 μm, negative), polyethylene nanoparticles **(PE 300)** (300 nm, negative), carboxylated polystyrene nanospheres **(carboxy PS)** (300 nm, negative), and amino-functionalized polystyrene nanospheres **(amino PS)** (200 nm, positive) were all purchased from Taobao (Hangzhou, China).

- 1.  _Preparation of polydopamine (PDA)-modified sodium alginate hydrogels_

Initially, sodium alginate and dopamine hydrochloride were indi-vidually added to distilled water and stirred at room temperature until fully dissolved, resulting in a 2 % _w_/_v_ sodium alginate solution and a 40 mg/mL dopamine hydrochloride solution. Subsequently, the sodium alginate solution (2 % _w_/_v_), dopamine hydrochloride solution (40 mg/ mL), and a 2 M sodium hydroxide solution were combined and stirred for 20 min **(**[Table 1](#_bookmark1)**)**. Next, the mixed solution was slowly added drop-wise to calcium chloride solution (2 % _w_/_v_) using a syringe. After 2-h incubation, polydopamine (PDA)-modified sodium alginate hydrogels were obtained **(PMSAH)**. Finally, the hydrogels were rinsed with distilled water to remove any unreacted crosslinking agents and un-linked polydopamine.

- 1.  _Characterizations_

Field emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM) was utilized for microstructures examination (Nano SEM-450; FEI, Hillsboro, OR, USA). The crystal structures of both sodium alginate hydrogels **(SAH)** and polydopamine (PDA)-modified sodium alginate hydrogels **(PMSAH)** were investigated using an X-ray diffractometer (D8 ADVANCE A25; Bruker, Germany). Dynamic light scattering (Malvern Instruments, Malvern, UK) was employed to analyze Zeta-potential. Fourier trans-form infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) was conducted on Vertex 70 Bruker (Vertex 70; Bruker, Ettlingen, Germany). Additionally, the hydrogels-forming solution was subjected to oscillatory frequency sweep experi-ments to determine the frequency-dependent behavior of the storage

(G′) and loss (G′′) moduli by Rheometers (DHR-1, Waters, USA). Thermal

stability was assessed through differential scanning calorimetry (DSC)

(Q2000, Waters, USA).

- 1.  _Determination of the swelling and deswelling properties_

Frozen-dried samples (0.2 g each) of samples were submerged in distilled water. Gel weights were measured for 8 h, with three parallel experiments conducted. Simultaneously, samples (2 g) were exposed to a 55 ◦C oven for dehydrating. The mass of the samples was regularly measured in three parallel experiments.

- 1.  _Preparation and characterizations of microplastics from tea bags_

A commercially available non-woven fabric tea bag was subjected to simulation under typical daily usage conditions. The tea bag was care-fully slit open to empty its contents, followed by three thorough rinses of the tea bag material using distilled water. Subsequently, the tea bags underwent immersion in hot water at 95 ◦C for 15 min to release any potential microplastics. After the heat treatment, the dispersed particles collected and lyophilized were scrutinized using scanning electron mi-croscopy (SEM) to identify any microplastics. The size distribution of microplastics and Zeta-potential analysis were determined using dy-namic light scattering (DLS).

- 1.  _Microplastics removal performance_

After soaking a non-woven tea bag in hot water (95 ◦C) for 15 min, 1 g of freeze-dried hydrogel microspheres were submerged in it for 2 h to ensure adequate adsorption. The quantification of microplastics in the solution before and after adsorption by hydrogels was conducted using a flow cytometer (FACSAria Special Order Researc, USA). Flow cytometry analysis was performed with SSC voltage set at 25 V, FSC voltage at 0 V, a flow rate of 15 μL min—1, and a collection time of 1 min. Data were analyzed to obtain the mean ± SD of three independent measurements \[[1](#_bookmark11)\]. The removal efficiency (R) of hydrogels for microplastics were determined by the following formula, respectively:

R (%) = _N_0 — _Nt_ × 100 (1)

_N_0

where _N_0 and _N_t are the initial and residual number of microplastics, respectively.

- 1.  _Adsorption mechanism assessment_

Different surface charges (negative or positive) and sizes (200 nm-10 μm) of microplastics were employed to investigate the capturing mechanism of PDA-modified hydrogels. The removal efficiency of hydrogels for various microplastics was determined based on the aforementioned methods. PDA-modified sodium alginate hydrogels after adsorbing microplastics were further characterizations by scanning electron microscopy (SEM), Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), and dynamic light scattering.

- 1.  _Adsorption isotherms and kinetics experiments_

In our investigation of adsorption isotherms, we examined carbox-ylated polystyrene nanospheres and amino-functionalized polystyrene nanospheres. The experiments were conducted in a thermostatic oscil-lator at 25 ◦C, for 2 h, using approximately 1 g of lyophilized hydrogel in 10 mL microplastics solution with initial concentrations ranging from 1 to 25 mg/mL. For the analysis of the adsorption isotherm data, we applied nonlinear forms of the Freundlich and Langmuir isotherm models.

- 1.  _Statistical analysis_

Results are presented as mean ± standard deviation of three inde-pendent experiments. Analysis of variance (ANOVA) was performed using SPSS software and _p_ < 0.05 indicates statistical significance.

# Results and discussion

- 1.  _Characterization of SAH and PMSAH_

Sodium alginate is a polycarboxylic acid containing numerous carboxyl groups (COO—) in its molecular structure. Upon contact with

multivalent cations such as calcium ions, an ion exchange process oc-curs, where the multivalent cations interact with the negatively charged carboxyl groups \[[11](#_bookmark21)\]. This strengthened attraction drives the gradual formation of a stable and reversible three-dimensional network struc-ture. It is well-known that sodium alginate-calcium ion hydrogels

possess a porous structure, which enhances their ability to absorb water, facilitate solution exchange, and promote molecular diffusion, making them particularly effective for capturing microplastics in water \[[12](#_bookmark22)\]. The formation of polydopamine chains is induced by the catalytic in-fluence of hydroxide ions on the phenolic groups (OH—) within dopa-mine molecules under alkaline conditions \[[6](#_bookmark16)\]. This process leads to a polymerization reaction, resulting in the establishment of covalent bonds between dopamine molecules and the generation of a polydop-amine chain \[[6](#_bookmark16)\]. For the preparation of polydopamine (PDA)-modified sodium alginate hydrogels **(PMSAH)**, the integration of PDA fibers oc-curs during the formation process of sodium alginate hydrogels. In [Fig. 1](#_bookmark2)A, we can see the freshly prepared SAH and PMSAH hydrogel beads. The SAH gel beads exhibited a spherical shape and are white, while the PMSAH beads were black. This color difference arised due to the oxidation process of polydopamine, where the phenolic groups within dopamine molecules transformed into quinone groups, forming the polymer and resulting in the production of a black-colored substance \[[13](#_bookmark23)\]. The size of the SAH and PMSAH hydrogel beads showed no sig-nificant difference, both measuring approximately 3.6 ± 0.83 mm. This is because hydrogels are fabricated by extruding through uniformly sized syringes into a crosslinking solution. Their larger size allowed for easy separation from drinking water after adsorbing microplastics. Zeta potential serves as a crucial parameter for gauging the electrical density of the gel network surface. The results indicated that both PDA and SAH surfaces carry a negative charge **(**[Fig. 1](#_bookmark2)B**)**. This was predominantly attributed to the plentiful hydroxyl groups (OH—) within the molecular structure of PDA and the abundant carboxyl groups (COO—) within the sodium alginate molecule \[[14](#_bookmark24)\]. With an increasing amount of PDA incorporated into the sodium alginate hydrogel, the zeta potential of PMSAH exhibited an upward trend, reaching a peak negative charge of

—19.63 ± 0.4 mV for PMSAH5.

- -   1.  _SEM_

The morphology of freeze-dried SAH and PMSAH hydrogel beads characterized by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) were shown in [Fig. 1](#_bookmark2)C. The presence of wrinkles and creases on the microbead surface was likely attributed to the freezing and evaporation of water during the freeze-drying process, coupled with the synergistic influence of the hydrogel network \[[11](#_bookmark21)\]. The beads exhibited a uniform dense surface structure without micropores, indicative of the stable characteristics of this hydrogel. Some research reported that the incorporation of a polyphenol-metal network or soybean protein nanofibers into the so-dium alginate hydrogel all resulted in reduced pore size, enhanced crosslinking density, and improved mechanical properties \[[14](#_bookmark24),[15](#_bookmark25)\]. The introduction of PDA resulted in more fibrous folds on the surface of PMSAH5. This was consistent with previous findings that polydopamine synthesized fiber with an average diameter of ~1.2 μm under alkaline conditions \[[6](#_bookmark16)\]. To verify the distribution of PDA fibers within the hydrogel, SEM-EDX images were captured. As depicted in [Fig. 2](#_bookmark3), the delineation of C and O elements maps the distribution of the gel framework, with the uniform presence of N elements providing evidence for the even distribution of PDA fibers.

- -   1.  _FTIR_

The infrared spectroscopy was used to demonstrate the intra-molecular and intermolecular interactions of SAH and PMSAH. The infrared spectra of sodium alginate and hydrochloride dopamine revealed distinctive peaks that provided valuable insights into their

molecular compositions **(**[Fig. 3](#_bookmark4)A-B**)**. In sodium alginate, the peak at 3200–3600 cm—1 indicated the stretching vibration of O–H bonds, suggesting the presence of hydroxyl groups (–OH) \[[16](#_bookmark26)\]. Additionally,

Furthermore, sodium alginate exhibits peaks around 1604.5 cm—1 and 1363.4 cm—1, associated with the asymmetric and symmetric stretching vibrations of the COO— functional group, respectively \[[17](#_bookmark27)\]. In the case of hydro-chloride dopamine, the vibration peak at 1271 cm—1 suggested the ab-sorption of the C–O bond within the dopamine phenol structure, and

the peak at 1606 cm—1 corresponded to the absorption of the C–C bond in the same structure. Additionally, the peak at 3313 cm—1 indicated stretching vibrations of N–H bonds and –OH bonds, while the vibration peak at 1514 cm—1 signified N–H bending vibrations \[[18](#_bookmark28)\]. The FTIR spectrum of sodium alginate hydrogel (SAH) closely resembled that of pure sodium alginate. Nevertheless, the observed increase in the in-tensity of stretching vibration peaks related to O–H bonds, C–O–C bonds, –C–H bonds, and C–O–C bonds indicated the presence of

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Fig. 3. (A-B)** FTIR spectra of SAH, PMSAH5, sodium alginate, and dopamine hydrochloride. **(C)** X-ray diffraction patterns of SAH, and PMSAH1 ~ PMSAH5. **(D)** DSC curves of SAH, and PMSAH1 ~ PMSAH5.

hydrogen bonding or hydrophobic interaction, suggesting the formation of the hydrogel structure \[[19](#_bookmark29)\]. The infrared spectrum of PMSAH5 exhibited a widening and intensification of the stretching vibration peak associated with O–H bonds, along with a notably enhanced shoulder peak observed at 2360.6 cm—1. The broadening and increased intensity of the O–H stretching vibration peak suggest modifications in the hydrogen bonding environment, likely attributed to the formation of hydrogen bonds between the -COOH groups of sodium alginate (SA) and the -OH groups of polydopamine (PDA) \[[20](#_bookmark30)\]. Polydopamine (PDA), rich

in hydroxyl, amine, and quinone groups, effectively adsorbs CO₂, which normally absorbs near 2349 cm—1 in IR spectra \[[21](#_bookmark31)\]. PDA modification

enhances CO₂ adsorption, causing a shoulder peak around 2360 cm—1. The incorporation of polydopamine introduced hydrogen bonds and π-π

stacking, augmenting its adsorption capacity for microplastics through chemical bonding.

- -   1.  _XRD_

The crystallinity can be used to represent the ratio of the crystalline region in the hydrogels. As reported, sodium alginate (SA) exhibited a broad peak at 19.81◦, implying its amorphous nature \[[17](#_bookmark27)\]. Pristine dopamine exhibits a crystalline structure, leading to multiple diffraction peaks in their XRD pattern \[[22](#_bookmark32)\]. As shown in [Fig. 3](#_bookmark4)C, the XRD spectrum of SAH displayed distinct diffraction peaks at 32◦ and 46◦, suggesting the presence of a crystalline structure \[[23](#_bookmark33)\]. Upon examining PMSAH1 ~ 5, no noticeable peak shift was observed, but there was a notable in-crease in peak intensities at 32◦ and 46◦. Additionally, new diffraction

peaks emerged at 57◦. The absence of peak shifts in PMSAH indicated that the crystallographic positions remain relatively unchanged, while the heightened peak intensities at existing angles signified an enhancement in crystallinity \[[23](#_bookmark33)\]. The appearance of new peaks at 57◦ suggested potential structural modifications or the introduction of new crystallographic planes in PMSAH \[[20](#_bookmark30)\]. These results indicated the successful binding of polydopamine to sodium alginate.

- -   1.  _DSC_

Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) is employed to assess the thermal properties of hydrogels. The results of SAH, as illustrated in [Fig. 3](#_bookmark4)D, revealed a distinct endothermic peak at 137.63 ◦C, corre-sponding to the melting temperature of the hydrogels \[[24](#_bookmark34)\]. Although the melting temperature of PMSAH1 ~ 5 remained relatively unchanged, there was a noticeable increase in the peak area. Specifically, the peak area increased from 245.1 J/g for SAH to 344 J/g for PMSAH 5 **(**Table S1**)**. The stable peak position implied an unchanged transition temperature, while the enlarged peak area suggested increased energy absorption, possibly due to a higher number of chemical bonds and the stronger hydrogen bonding forces or electrostatic attractions present in PMSAH \[[25](#_bookmark35)\]. The consistency of this result with the findings from FTIR and XRD studies confirmed the successful integration of PDA fibers into the sodium alginate hydrogel. Polydopamine-modified sodium alginate hydrogel exhibited higher thermal stability.

- -   1.  _Rheological analysis_

The dynamic rheological performance of hydrogels serves as a reflection of their viscoelastic nature. The storage modulus (G′) mirrors the elastic properties, indicating the gel’s ability to recover its initial shape. Conversely, the loss modulus (G″) characterizes the viscous na-ture, highlighting the gel’s ability to undergo irreversible deformations

\[[14](#_bookmark24)\]. As evident from [Fig. 4](#_bookmark5)A-B, the pronounced predominance of the loss modulus over the storage modulus was observable. This observation pointed to a scenario where viscous deformation played a predominant

role in the hydrogels-forming solution \[[14](#_bookmark24)\]. Prior investigations consistently revealed that the storage modulus profile (G′) consistently exceeded the loss modulus profile (G″) across all hydrogels examined.

This consistent trend indicated the establishment of a sturdy three-dimensional mesh structure within the hydrogels \[[20](#_bookmark30),[26](#_bookmark36)\]. In our study, we noted a rise in the storage modulus of PMSAH5-forming so-lution in comparison to SAH-forming solution, accompanied by a reduction in the loss modulus. This observation implied a transition towards a more elastic behavior in PMSAH5-forming solution, suggest-ing the structural influence of PDA fibers may play a role in reinforcing the elastic characteristics of PMSAH5-forming solution. The heightened elastic properties observed in the PMSAH5-forming solution serve as a foundational element for producing hydrogels with superior elasticity.

- -   1.  _Swelling and water retention properties_

We characterized the swelling behavior of the hydrogels through

measuring the mass change after water absorption. As depicted in [Fig. 4](#_bookmark5)C, no observable swelling was detected for all hydrogels within the first 6 h of immersion in distilled water (DW). The lower swelling behavior observed in the hydrogel may be attributed to the presence of a crystalline structure within the material \[[27](#_bookmark37)\]. The formation of crys-talline structures often hinders the permeation of water molecules, thereby diminishing the material’s water absorption capacity \[[27](#_bookmark37)\]. The diminished swelling observed in our study stands in contrast to earlier research that documented the rapid water absorption and swelling of hydrogels (ranging from 38 % to 78 %) within a two-hour timeframe \[[20](#_bookmark30),[26](#_bookmark36)\]. This could be attributed to a heightened number of effective cross-linking points in the microsphere-type sodium alginate hydrogel, impeding the ingress of water molecules \[[28](#_bookmark38)\]. After prolonged soaking for 8 h, SAH exhibited an increase in mass, while PMSAH did not display any swelling behavior. Other studies have similarly found that incor-porating PDA leads to a reduction in the swelling properties of hydrogels \[[6](#_bookmark16)\]. This phenomenon may be attributed to an increase in physical cross-linking points and tighter structure, thereby restricting the expansion of the porous structure and limiting the rate of water absorption \[[6](#_bookmark16)\]. The diminished swelling capacity makes it advantageous for the adsorption of microplastics in tea broth. This results in a more stable structure without compromising the quality of the tea infusion.

As depicted in [Fig. 4](#_bookmark5)D, after a 30-h drying period at 55 ◦C, all

hydrogels undergo complete water loss. Notably, these hydrogels showed superior water retention capabilities in comparison to those

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Fig. 4. (A-B)** Rheological analysis curves of hydrogels-forming solution of SAH, and PMSAH1 ~ PMSAH5. **(C**–**D)** Water retention and Swelling properties of SAH, and PMSAH1 ~ PMSAH5.

reported in other researches. Specifically, the salecan hydrogel, incor-porating poly (ethylene glycol) diglycidyl ether (PEGDGE) as the cross-linking agent, experienced full moisture loss following a 400-min drying period at 37 ◦C \[[6](#_bookmark16)\]. Interestingly, the introduction of PDA fibers did not show a significant alteration in the water retention capacity of the hydrogel. This differed from previous research findings that reported an increase in water retention capacity with the incorporation of PDA fi-bers, attributed to their abundance of hydrophilic functional groups \[[6](#_bookmark16)\]. Similar studies have also reported that the introduction of metal-phenolic networks results in an increased water retention capacity of sodium alginate hydrogels cross-linked by calcium ions \[[20](#_bookmark30)\]. Metal-phenolic networks, rich in hydrophilic functional groups, also contribute to a denser hydrogel structure, consequently reducing the loss of moisture \[[20](#_bookmark30)\].

- 1.  _Microplastics removal performance_

As a common source of microplastics in daily consumption, particles released from non-woven fabric tea bags after 15 min of immersion in hot water (95 ◦C) were analyzed for their shape and size using SEM. In

[Fig. 5](#_bookmark6)A, the presence of irregularly shaped and relatively large aggre-gates was evident. Moreover, the identification of smaller individual particles in close proximity to these aggregates served as conclusive evidence for the release of microplastics from the tea bag. Subsequently, we conducted measurements on the particle size and zeta potential of these microplastic particles. The results unveiled an average particle size of approximately 424.13 ± 19.29 nm, with the particles displaying a negative charge of around —17.9 ± 2.21 mV ([Fig. 5](#_bookmark6)B-C**)**. Similar studies have reported the release of microplastics from polypropylene (PP)-based tea bags, consisting of irregular particles with sizes ranging from

0.1 to 1.5 μm \[[1](#_bookmark11)\]. Additionally, it was reported that smaller micro-plastics released from commercial tea bags, measuring approximately 102 ± 22 nm to 357 ± 156 nm \[[29](#_bookmark39)\]. Flow cytometry was employed to quantify the number of nanoparticles in the tea bag infusion before and after adsorption by PMSAH5. As illustrated in [Fig. 5](#_bookmark6)D-E, a noticeable reduction in particles was observed after the adsorption by the hydrogel, indicating the superior capturing performance of PMSAH5. Specifically, the removal efficiency of SAH and PMSAH1–5 for microplastic particles was depicted in [Fig. 5](#_bookmark6)F. It is evident that, following PDA modification, sodium alginate hydrogels exhibited a significantly enhanced removal

5 for microplastics ([Fig. 5](#_bookmark6)G**)**. Therefore, subsequent experiments will focus on using PMSAH 5 to investigate its adsorption characteristics for microplastics.

- 1.  _Adsorption characteristics analysis_

To understand whether microplastics were captured through phys-ical interception or chemical adsorption, and if electrostatic interactions play a predominant role in the adsorption process. Different surface charges (negative or positive) and sizes (200 nm-10 μm) of microplastics were employed to investigate the capturing mechanism of PDA-modified hydrogels. Various microplastic particles not only differ significantly in composition but also possess distinct surface charges and particle sizes. Specifically, polyethylene microspheres **(PE 10)** (10 μm, negative), polyethylene nanoparticles **(PE 300)** (300 nm, negative), carboxylated polystyrene nanospheres **(carboxy PS)** (300 nm, negative), and amino-functionalized polystyrene nanospheres **(amino PS)** (200 nm, positive) were examined. Following polydopamine modification, PMSAH5 exhibited a heightened surface negative charge. As anticipated, the negatively charged PMSAH5 effectively removed amino-functionalized polystyrene nanospheres (amino PS) (200 nm, positive) due to strong electrostatic interactions between surfaces with opposite charges **(**[Fig. 6](#_bookmark7)A). Surprisingly, microplastics with negative charges, such as polyethylene microspheres (PE 10) (10 μm, negative), polyethylene nanoparticles (PE 300) (300 nm, negative), and carboxylated poly-styrene nanospheres (carboxy PS) (300 nm, negative), were captured on the negatively charged surface of PMSAH5. This contradicts the initial expectation of weak attraction or even repulsion between surfaces with similar charges. This phenomenon suggested that, in addition to elec-trostatic interactions, other types of interfacial molecular interactions contributed to the capture of microplastics. Moreover, the zeta potential of PMSAH5 after adsorbing various microplastics indicated that micro-plastic particles with different charges influenced the surface charge of the hydrogel ([Fig. 6](#_bookmark7)B**)**. This confirmed that the hydrogel successfully adsorbed microplastics, regardless of their size and surface charge. This adsorption was driven by the combined action of multiple forces.

The FTIR analysis of PMSAH5 before and after various microplastics

adsorption were shown in [Fig. 6](#_bookmark7)C-D. The broadening and increased in-tensity observed in the –OH stretching vibration peak at 3434.5 cm—1, along with the asymmetric and symmetric stretching vibrations of the COO— functional group at 1604.5 cm—1 and 1356.9 cm—1, in comparison to the pure PMSAH form, collectively pointed towards the presence of hydrogen bonding interactions within various functional groups of the hydrogel \[[6](#_bookmark16)\]. Following the adsorption onto PMSAH5, the characteristic peaks between 2800 and 3000 cm—1 associated with C–H bonds on microplastic particles exhibited varying degrees of intensity changes. This observation signified the formation of hydrogen bonds and π-π in-teractions between PMSAH5 and microplastic particles during the adsorption process \[[30](#_bookmark40)\]. As was well-known, the multiple phenolic and amine groups in polydopamine provided it with the ability to form hydrogen bonds, van der Waals forces, and salt bridges with various

surfaces, thereby enhancing its adhesive capabilities \[[10](#_bookmark20)\]. As reported, the electron-rich π-conjugated orbitals within the aromatic ring of polystyrene (PS) played an active role in forming π-π interactions with polyphenol molecules \[[1](#_bookmark11)\]. Furthermore, these polyphenols impart the PMSAH5 surface with an abundance of aromatic rings, creating an enticing hydrophobic substrate for the carbon-chain various micro-plastic backbone (i.e., PS, PE, PVC, and PP) \[[1](#_bookmark11)\]. This intricate interplay of molecular interactions underscored the adhesive prowess of PMSAH5 in effectively capturing microplastics. Similar studies have reported that polydopamine-modified salecan hydrogels have shown an enhanced capacity for the adsorption of antibiotics \[[6](#_bookmark16)\]. Additionally, it was re-ported functionalized wood sawdust with tannic acid (TA) and Fe3+ was effective in removing microplastics from water \[[1](#_bookmark11)\]. These findings suggest that phenolic groups provide a means to generate strong inter-facial forces that drive the adsorption and capture processes of polymer

particles, including non-biodegradable microplastics.

Based on the above results, we proposed a potential adsorption mechanism for PMSAH. PMSAH seemed to attract not only positively charged microplastic particles through electrostatic interactions but also to form non-covalent bonds, such as hydrogen bonds and π-π in-teractions, with the benzene rings and hydroxyl groups of PMSAH and the molecules of negatively charged microplastics. Electrostatic in-teractions primarily occur between charged functional groups, such as amino groups (—NH2), carboxyl groups (-COOH), and other ionic groups. The attraction between positively and negatively charged sites facilitates the adsorption of molecules onto surfaces \[[30](#_bookmark40)\]. Hydrogen bonding happens between polar functional groups that have hydrogen atoms bonded to electronegative atoms (like oxygen or nitrogen). Common groups involved in hydrogen bonding include hydroxyl groups (-OH), carbonyl groups (C=O), and amine groups (-NH2). These in-teractions play a crucial role in stabilizing the adsorbed species. π-π Stacking occurs between aromatic rings or other π-conjugated systems \[[6](#_bookmark16)\]. The interactions involve the overlap of π orbitals from aromatic compounds, such as benzene rings, and are significant in the adsorption of organic molecules containing π-electron systems, such as phenolic compounds or certain dyes \[[30](#_bookmark40)\]. These interactions collectively contribute to the overall process of adsorption by enhancing the binding affinity of the different microplastics to the surface.

The typical SEM images of carboxylated polystyrene (carboxyl PS) particles subjected to PMSAH5 adsorption was shown in [Fig. 6](#_bookmark7)E**.** Nanoplastic particles adhered to the surface of the hydrogel, exhibiting a tendency to cluster and form multiple layers during adsorption, rather than forming a uniform monolayer. Hence, we speculated that the adsorption of PMSAH5 onto microplastics was concentration-dependent, showing an escalating trend in adsorption quantity with increasing concentrations. Moreover, there appeared to be a variety of adsorption sites.

- 1.  _Adsorption kinetics and isotherms analysis_

To better understand how PMSAH5 adhered to amino-functionalized and carboxylated polystyrene nanospheres, we conducted measure-ments and analyzed the adsorption kinetics employing the pseudo-first-order (PFO) and pseudo-second-order (PSO) models. PFO assumes a linear relationship with respect to time, while PSO considers the square of the unoccupied sites. Usually, experimental data exhibit better cor-relation with the PSO model, particularly in systems with chemisorption \[[31](#_bookmark41)\]. Hydrogels exhibited rapid initial adsorption of microplastic par-ticles, reaching equilibrium after 2 h. As shown in [Fig. 7](#_bookmark8)A-B and [Table 2](#_bookmark9), for Amino-functionalized polystyrene, the PSO model, with correlation

coefficients (R2) > 0.989, proved more accurate than the PFO model (R2

\> 0.849). Similarly, in Carboxylated polystyrene, the PSO model, with R2 > 0.994, outperformed the PFO model (R2 > 0.989). The preference for the pseudo-second-order kinetics suggested multiple adsorption

sites, indicating potential chemical reactions beyond physical adsorp-tion. These reactions may involve the formation of chemical bonds or other interactions \[[31](#_bookmark41)\].

Adsorption isotherms play a crucial role in unraveling the intricacies of adsorption interactions and determining the maximum adsorption capacity \[[30](#_bookmark40)\]. As the initial concentration of microplastics increased, there was a corresponding elevation in the adsorption capacity of PMSAH5 ([Fig. 7](#_bookmark8)C-D**)**. This augmentation was attributed to the height-ened driving force overcoming mass transfer resistance between the aqueous phase and solid phase with the escalating concentration of microplastics \[[6](#_bookmark16)\]. Experimental data, represented by Qe and Ce, were fitted to non-linear Langmuir and Freundlich models. The Langmuir model assumes monolayer adsorption with a uniform surface, while the Freundlich model allows for multilayer adsorption on a heterogeneous surface \[[33](#_bookmark43)\]. The correlation results, as shown in [Table 3](#_bookmark10), indicated that the R2 values for the Freundlich model (0.994–0.999) surpassed those of the Langmuir model (with R2 values ranging from 0.988 to 0.997). findings suggested that the adsorption of microplastics by PMSAH5 aligned more closely with the Freundlich model, indicative of multilayer adsorption \[[32](#_bookmark42)\]. In the Freundlich isotherm, the curve displays a loga-rithmic relationship, appearing linear at lower concentrations and gradually saturating at higher concentrations. This aligns with a

multilayer adsorption scenario, where on a non-uniform surface, adsorbate molecules gradually occupy available adsorption sites, resulting in saturation effects \[[33](#_bookmark43)\].

# Conclusions and limitation

In summary, our study unveiled a straightforward, versatile, and environmentally conscious strategy for microplastics removal, incor-porating calcium ions as a chemical cross-linker and modifying sodium alginate with PDA fibers. A comprehensive exploration of the physico-chemical properties and adsorption performance of both SAH and PMSAH was undertaken. The incorporation of polydopamine reduced the hydrogel’s surface zeta potential and increased its adsorption ca-pacity for microplastics. PMSAH5 exhibited the highest removal effi-ciency, reaching approximately 99.6 %. Additionally, polydopamine-

modified sodium alginate hydrogel exhibited higher elasticity and thermal stability. The hydrogel successfully adsorbed microplastics, regardless of their size and surface charge. This adsorption was driven by the combined action of multiple forces, resulting in multilayer adsorption. Moreover, hydrogels exhibited rapid initial adsorption of microplastic particles, reaching equilibrium after 2 h. Notably, it dis-played substantial maximum adsorption capacities of 127.98 mg/g for Amino-functionalized polystyrene and 154.57 mg/g for Carboxylated polystyrene. Furthermore, its microplastic adsorption process closely conformed to the PSO model, with a more pronounced fit to the Freundlich model during isothermal adsorption. The primary mecha-nisms governing PMSAH5’s microplastic adsorption involved chemical adsorption and electrostatic interactions, influenced by factors like hydrogen bonding and π-π interactions.

Although this material effectively removes microplastics released from tea bags in simulated tea solutions, numerous studies have re-ported that sodium alginate-calcium chloride hydrogels exhibit greater structural stability at acidic pH but tend to rupture under alkaline conditions \[[34](#_bookmark44)\]. Consequently, the PMSAH prepared in this study is not

suitable for use in alkaline environments. In the future research, mate-rials capable of effectively removing microplastics in different food products (varying pH levels and osmotic pressures) should be thor-oughly investigated. Additionally, the effectiveness of these materials in removing other harmful substances, such as antibiotics and toxins pre-sent in fruit juices, should be explored to further expand their broad applicability.
